newsitem.title: UK: N Korea could face mass starvation if crops fail.
newsitem.headline: N Korea could face mass starvation if crops fail.

text.p: Widespread hunger in North Korea can only get worse before the autumn harvest and could develop into mass starvation if not enough international food aid is sent soon, a senior U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) official said on Friday.
"Mass starvation is possible but I hope it can be avoided," said Rolf Huss, the WFP's senior desk officer for North Korea, after a three-week visit to the highly secretive country.
"Things have definitely gone from bad to much worse since when I visited in March," the Rome-based Huss told Reuters.
"There are general food shortages. Everyone in the country is affected to some extent. All you see is slim people. There is absolutely no one carrying any extra weight."
"Things are going to get worse for the next few months till the harvest in October."
Huss said the greatest danger was that if sufficient food aid did not materialise in time and the maize harvest was gathered early when it was still green, as happened last year.
"Maize develops very quickly at the end of the cycle. If it is harvested two weeks too early, you lose half of the volume.
"That creates a downward spiral because there will be no food stocks as a result."
But Huss said there was hope that this could be avoided and he was encouraged by donors' speedy response to the U.N.'s latest appeal for aid for North Korea.
Donors have already met almost one third of a new $46 million appeal, WFP executive director Catherine Bertini said on Thursday.
The WFP has distributed harrowing pictures of pale, hungry children, some reduced to near skeletons, and Huss said such cases were widespread, even in the showcase capital, Pyongyang.
The immediate cause of the famine was disastrous floods just before the harvest in 1995 and again last year, although Western officials say rigid Stalinist central planning is also to blame.
North Korea has so far refused virtually all foreign journalists' requests for visas and WFP and other aid officials are almost the only source of information about the famine.

Huss said the WFP was targeting 4.7 million people out of a population of 23 million, with a special focus on children. The international Red Cross and other organisations were targeting about one million more, he added.
Huss said the communist government, which prides itself on its ideological purity, was showing some flexibility in face of the famine. It now allowed small-scale private food stalls in many towns.

North Korea surprised the world in 1995 when it requested international aid after the floods. It had previously adhered rigidly to its doctrine of "juche" or self-sufficiency and had condemned offers of international aid as a threat to its national security.

Huss, a Swede, said North Korean officials were cooperating well with the WFP, which now had 15 international officers in the country, compared with just one when it first set up an office in Pyongyang in 1995.
The WFP was leasing a Russian helicopter from the North Korean civil aviation authorities, although fuel was sometimes a problem, he added.
He said WFP staff had to obtain permission to travel around the country, and that North Korean disaster relief officials had to refer their requests to the military before giving the go-ahead.
But they were generally able to visit all areas where WFP food was being distributed. "They accept the principle that we must have access where food is distributed," Huss said.
